comparisons.peer_summary: Micron makes significant investments in proprietary product and process technology to increase bit density and reduce costs, introducing new generations with improved performance characteristics such as higher data transfer rates, advanced packaging, lower power consumption, and increased memory density.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and Micron explicitly link their manufacturing and process technology investments to the economic benefits of Moore's Law, specifically aiming to reduce per-unit costs and increase performance/density through new product generations. Intel states that realizing Moore's Law allows it to 'reduce a chip's cost as we shrink its size or increase functionality... while maintaining the same cost,' with core products on Intel 7, 4, and 3 nodes. Similarly, Micron notes that its 'significant investments to develop proprietary product and process technology... generally increases bit density per wafer and reduces per-bit manufacturing costs,' introducing new generations with improved characteristics like higher density.

sentences.text: We continue to develop new generations of manufacturing process technology as we seek to realize the benefits from Moore's Law, a law of economics predicted by Intel's cofounder Gordon Moore more than 50 years ago.

Realizing Moore's Law results in economic benefits as we are able to either reduce a chip's cost as we shrink its size or increase functionality and performance of a chip while maintaining the same cost with higher density.

We make significant investments to develop proprietary product and process technology, which generally increases bit density per wafer and reduces per-bit manufacturing costs of each generation of product.

We continue to introduce new generations of products that offer improved performance characteristics, including higher data transfer rates, advanced packaging solutions, lower power consumption, improved read/write reliability, and increased memory density.

comparisons.peer_topic: DRAM production nodes and future expectations
comparisons.peer_summary: The company shipped its industry's first 1β production node in 2023, produced majority 2024 bits on 1α and 1β nodes, and expects volume shipments of the 1γ node using EUV lithography in 2025.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures detail the specific advancement of manufacturing process nodes as a key strategic driver. Intel identifies its 'Intel 7, Intel 4 and Intel 3 process nodes' as the technologies for its 2024 core products, with Intel 4 and 3 ramping to high volume. Micron details its specific DRAM node progression, stating it shipped the 'industry's first 1β production node in 2023,' produced the majority of 2024 bits on '1α and 1β nodes,' and expects volume shipments of the '1γ' node in 2025.

sentences.text: As of the end of 2024, our core products were manufactured on 300mm wafers, with a significant majority manufactured using our Intel 7 process node while we ramped our Intel 4 and Intel 3 process nodes into high volume.
In 2023, we began shipping the industry's first 1β (1-beta) production node, which offers further improvements in power efficiency and bit density.
The majority of our DRAM bit production in 2024 was on leading-edge 1α (1-alpha) and 1ß nodes.

comparisons.peer_summary: NVIDIA advances its business through a unified accelerated computing platform leveraging GPUs, CUDA, and networking technologies to solve complex problems with performance leaps that outpace Moore's Law across Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive markets.
comparisons.comparison: Both Intel and NVIDIA explicitly reference Moore's Law as a benchmark for performance and cost optimization, though they describe their innovation strategies differently. Intel describes realizing Moore's Law as an 'economic benefit' achieved by 'reduce[ing] a chip's cost as we shrink its size or increase functionality.' In contrast, NVIDIA states its strategy is to 'deliver continued performance leaps that outpace Moore's Law' through 'full-stack innovation' across architecture, design, and software, rather than relying solely on geometric shrinking.
